prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency standards of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a concrete, original idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms so that the light shift cancels) that was demonstrated and then pushed by about two orders of magnitude beyond the caesium standard, to roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. It rests on controlled atomic physics: the choice of the magic wavelength, blackbody, hyperfine and higher-order light shifts, and collisional effects all had to be understood quantitatively before the accuracy claims could be trusted. It has been independently reproduced by several laboratories, it is the basis of the roadmap toward a redefinition of the second, and it opens tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and relativistic geodesy. The attribution is unusually clean: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking the clock to record accuracy and for the many-body clock. That the candidate was ranked first by Kroll and me, and in the top five by Johansson, Olsson, Pearce and Danielsson, is not itself the argument; the argument is that it is mature, well attributed and distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a committee could read this as technique refinement building on prizes already given for the frequency comb (2005) and for single-ion control (2012), and as an invention whose full consequence, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. Priority for the magic-wavelength concept is also shared with other proposers, and strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups (for example in Paris, Boulder and Braunschweig) contributed essential systematic-uncertainty work that a two-name prize cannot represent. Finally, Ye appears in a second candidate (B014), which weakens the perception of breadth if the committee wants to avoid concentrating recognition. I rate B046 and B038 as the nearest rivals in scientific weight, and I would not call B041 a certain winner.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first because the principle is easy to state, accuracy improved by about two orders of magnitude over caesium, the attribution to Katori and Ye is clean, and several laboratories reproduce the performance.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and the reproducibility argument, but I would not rest the case on the ease of stating the principle. The part that makes this physics rather than engineering is the atomic-structure control behind the accuracy budget, and that is what I would put in the citation. I also take more seriously than Kroll does the point that the 2005 comb link may be read as overlap: I think the answer is that the comb provides the counting of optical cycles while the lattice clock provides the new atomic reference, which is a distinct achievement, but we should state this explicitly rather than assume it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald confirmed by a decisive experiment from Jarillo-Herrero, creating a widely imitated platform, and ranks the lattice clock only fifth.
responses.response: I agree that B046 is among the most influential recent discoveries and I ranked it third myself. My disagreement is about timing and completeness. Mehlig and Johansson both note that the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved and the field is about eight years old, and the experimental credit (Cao and the first-author group, Dean, Yacoby, Young and others) is difficult to cover with one credited experimentalist. The clock has a longer, stable record and a settled attribution. I do not think the opening support for B046 shows it is more deserving, only that it is exciting; I would keep it as my first alternative rather than the preferred choice.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems (B030) first as an original, conceptually clean framework that is experimentally verified and mature, while placing twisted bilayer graphene last of eight as possibly premature.
responses.response: I share Mehlig's concern about prematurity for B046, and that is part of why I keep B041 ahead of it. I am less persuaded on B030: Mehlig himself says the priority among Evans, Searles, Cohen, Gallavotti, Jarzynski and Crooks is contested, and asks whether the experiments test more than ordinary thermodynamics implies. A prize whose allocation cannot be defended with the credited names is the weaker candidate even if the idea is elegant, and it received support from only one member. I would want to hear a specific argument for the two-name Jarzynski and Evans core before moving it up.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy (B033) first, as an instrument plus discovery that is timely, and notes that Jun Ye appears in other candidates so the committee might avoid repeating emphasis on a single laureate.
responses.response: The Ye point is fair, and I accept it as a real uncertainty, though I think it argues for care in which Ye achievement is cited rather than against B041: the lattice clock is the achievement for which he is most clearly credited. On B033, I recognise the discovery is firm, but I am concerned, as Danielsson also notes, that source identification is incomplete and the credit for a collaboration of hundreds rests on two names, one of which, Karle, I cannot judge from my own field. I would want more evidence from members closer to astroparticle physics before ranking it above the clock.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B031) first, while disclosing that it is her own subfield, and flags that a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 may be unwelcome.
responses.response: I value the disclosure and I agree that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling makes B031 sensitive in timing, though I regard it as a distinct discovery. My difficulty is the credit between the Blais proposal, the Wallraff demonstration and the Schoelkopf transmon and readout work, with Girvin outside the names. I would treat B031 as a serious later candidate rather than a first choice this year, but I would not argue against it on scientific grounds.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second, or considers demonstrated performance sufficient.
Whether the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes make a lattice-clock prize read as incremental to colleagues outside atomic physics.
Priority for the magic-wavelength idea and the weight of other strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups, which I am relying on memory for and have not verified.
Whether a two-name B041 prize could instead be paired with a second distinct achievement; I have not found a pairing that I can defend in terms of attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B041 (Katori, Ye) or for the alternatives B046 and B038. I do disclose my broader connections as an atomic theorist: a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund group and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH, and work with Reinhold Schuch and others. None of these people is a credited name in the preferred configuration or the named alternatives, but they would require recusal on any attosecond candidate if one were shortlisted.
